4.bulletin: An [[orbiter|orbiter]] just spotted a dust storm growing.

a.line: Dust blocks our sunlight, not the Sun's radiation. Build the wall now!

b.line: Keep the water for drinking. The Sun is calm today.

after.default: Dust blocks sunlight, so the panels make less power. It does not stop [[radiation|radiation]] from the Sun. A [[waterWall|water wall]] helps with that.

default: Why can't water do both jobs?

8.bulletin: The dust storm is getting closer. There's still time to go out.

a.line: Let's fetch ice before the water runs out!

b.line: Stay in and measure the dust. It's so rare!

ice: Uses power, and more radiation outside
bags: A thicker wall, no water used
Uses power, and more radiation outside

after.ice: You came back with [[ice|ice]]. Outside, though, the crew got more [[radiation|radiation]].
after.bags: The wall is thicker now. Outside, though, the crew got more [[radiation|radiation]].
after.science: Staying inside kept the crew safe, but the water did not grow.

ice: Got it! Our boots are dusty, but the tank is fuller.
bags: Heavy work, but the wall is thicker now!
science: Look at these dust grains under the microscope!

11.bulletin: Dust now covers the Sun. The solar panels barely get light.

a.line: Put every bit of power into heat and air!

b.line: A storm like this is rare. Save some power to study it!

safety: Warm, with plenty of air today
reserve: Colder, and less air is made

after.default: The thicker the dust, the less power the [[panels|solar panels]] make.

safety: Heaters on. Keep your jackets close, everyone.
science: Thank you! This storm data is gold.
reserve: Brr! Chilly, but the battery will last.

14.bulletin: Opportunity has gone silent. The [[dustLevel|dust level]] reached 10.8!

a.line: Without lights, our garden stops making food!

b.line: Those garden lamps eat too much power!

after.keep: The [[greenhouse|greenhouse]] keeps growing food, but it costs power every day.
after.off: No lights, no growing. The next days will have less food.
after.source: Opportunity ran on sunlight. With no sun, it could not recharge. Dust blocks sunlight but not cosmic [[radiation|radiation]]: Curiosity still measured about 9 [[doseUnit|units]] per hour during the storm (NASA RadLab).
after.dim: Half the light, half the food. A little less food in the next days.

keep: Thank you! The beans are still growing.
dim: They'll grow slower, but they'll grow.

17.bulletin: Beep beep! The [[radiation|radiation]] meter jumped. A [[solarStorm|solar storm]]?

a.line: Into the shelter, now! Don't wait!

b.line: Let's ask Earth first. It might be a false alarm!

shelter: Safest if the storm is real

after.real: It was real! The fastest bits arrived before Earth could even answer.
after.false: It was a [[falseAlarm|false alarm]]. Asking first saved power this time.
after.source: Real data from Curiosity (NASA RadLab): on a normal day at Gale Crater, radiation is about 8 [[doseUnit|units]] per hour. On 11 September 2017 it jumped to about 18, more than double!
after.falseShelter: It was a [[falseAlarm|false alarm]]. The [[shelter|shelter]] heaters used power for nothing.
after.clueWrong: The clue was wrong this time. Even good clues can trick us.

17.bulletinBoth: Beep beep! Both [[radiation|radiation]] meters jumped at once!
17.bulletinOne: Beep! One [[radiation|radiation]] meter jumped, but the other stayed quiet.

shelterFalse: Better safe than sorry. Next time, let's read the meters.

21.bulletin: The water tank is almost empty, and the dust is still here.

a.line: Let's take water back from the wall and drink it!

b.line: But what if another solar storm comes?

after.default: One part of water can't be a drink and a wall at the same time.

21.bulletinFull: The dust is still here. Do we still need the water wall?
21.aFull: We have water to spare. Take some back anyway?
21.bFull: Keep the wall. Another storm could come.

keep: Small sips, everyone. The wall stays.
keepFull: We have enough water. The wall stays.

26.bulletin: The storm now wraps around the whole planet.

a.line: Let's wipe the panels. Every bit of power helps!

b.line: We have a little power left. One last experiment!

clean: More radiation outside, and the Sun is weak

after.default: Clean panels still need sunshine, and the dust will stay for weeks.

clean: Shiny panels! Every bit of light helps.
burst: Last measurement saved. We made history!

sources.title: Where is this data from?
sources.kid: This station is imagined. Dust numbers come from Opportunity, radiation from Curiosity. The two rovers were in different places.

labels.based: Real, but moved to another day.
labels.game: A number that balances the game.

notes: The real storm lasted months. The game squeezes it into 30 days.
The dust level on 10 June 2018 is real: about 10.8 (one NASA figure shows 10.5). Other days are game numbers; the dust stays thick, as it did for weeks.
The Radiation bar is the game's dose budget, not NASA's real limit.
In 2018 the Sun was quiet. The game's solar storm is based on the September 2017 solar particle event.
Message delays come from JPL Horizons for each day.
Dust numbers come from Opportunity at Meridiani Planum. Radiation numbers come from Curiosity at Gale Crater, far away.
Dates use Earth calendar days in 2018. Each game day stands for one sol, which is 40 minutes longer.
words: A day on Mars. It lasts 24 hours and 40 minutes. Scientists call it a sol.
Tiny, super-fast bits from space. They pass through thin things; thick walls and water stop part of them. Too much can make people sick.
When the Sun suddenly throws out a huge burst of radiation. Scientists call it a solar particle event.
How thick the dust is. 1 is a little hazy. 10 is almost dark at noon.
A small room with thick walls where the crew hides from radiation.
The hydrogen in water stops part of the radiation. Water tanks around the shelter make a wall: more tanks, more protection, but no wall stops it all.
data: Opportunity's last dust level, about 10.8 on 10 June 2018 (one NASA figure shows 10.5): NASA/JPL
Radiation on Mars, September 2017: Curiosity RAD, Zeitlin et al. 2018
Earth–Mars distance for each day: JPL Horizons
Planet-wide dust after June 2018: Montabone et al. 2020
The September 2017 solar storm in DONKI (X8.2 flare, 10 Sep 2017)
Where Opportunity (Meridiani) and Curiosity (Gale) are: NASA Mars Trek
Radiation on Mars measured by Curiosity: RAD data in NASA OSDR RadLab
Storm shelters with water walls can cut the radiation dose by about half: NASA RadWorks study (NTRS 20150001237)
Real experiments on young plants and space-like radiation: NASA OSDR (OSD-46)

cutscene.text: This is Mars, the red planet. The year is 2018.
One June morning, a little cloud of [[dust|dust]] began to grow.
It grew and grew, until dust hid the Sun all over Mars.
Opportunity, a robot [[rover|rover]] that ran on sunlight, fell asleep. It never woke up.
Now imagine a team of explorers living on Mars that summer.
You are their Commander. Keep everyone safe for 30 days.
A Mars day is called a [[sol|sol]]. It is 40 minutes longer than ours.
Every choice has a cost. Ready, Commander?

howto.title: 1. Read the news
howto.text: Each choice starts with the news and two crew members who disagree.

howto.title: 2. Pick a card
howto.text: Every card shows what you gain and what it costs.

howto.title: 3. Watch the bars
howto.text: Life (tap for oxygen, water, food) and Power: keep them high. Radiation: keep it low.

howto.title: 4. Water does one job
howto.text: Water is for drinking or for the radiation wall, never both.

howto.title: 5. Earth is far away
howto.text: A message to Earth takes minutes. Sometimes you must decide alone.

howto.title: 6. Real or game?
howto.text: Labels show what is real NASA data and what is a game number.

howto.title: 7. Tricky words
howto.text: Tap a dotted word to learn what it means.

howto.title: 8. Reach day 30
howto.text: Keep everyone safe until help comes. Then see what one different choice would change.

glossary.sol: A day on Mars. It lasts 24 hours and 40 minutes. Scientists call it a sol.
glossary.radiation: Tiny, super-fast bits from space. They pass through thin things; thick walls and water stop part of them. Too much can make people sick.
glossary.solarStorm: When the Sun suddenly throws out a huge burst of radiation. Scientists call it a solar particle event.
glossary.dust: Mars dust storms can cover the whole planet. Dust blocks sunlight, but it does not bring radiation.
glossary.dustLevel: How thick the dust is. 1 is a little hazy. 10 is almost dark at noon.
glossary.rover: A robot car that drives around Mars and studies it.
glossary.orbiter: A spacecraft that circles Mars and takes pictures from above.
glossary.shelter: A small room with thick walls where the crew hides from radiation.
glossary.waterWall: The hydrogen in water stops part of the radiation. Water tanks around the shelter make a wall: more tanks, more protection, but no wall stops it all.
glossary.panels: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity.
glossary.greenhouse: A glass garden where the crew grows food under lamps.
glossary.delay: Messages fly as fast as light, but Mars is so far away that they still take minutes.
glossary.oxygen: The air we breathe. The station makes it with electricity.
glossary.falseAlarm: When an alarm goes off but nothing dangerous is really happening.
glossary.ice: Mars has frozen water under the ground. Melt it, and you can drink it.
glossary.doseUnit: Micro-gray per hour (µGy/h): how much radiation a body soaks up each hour. A bigger number means more radiation.
